newsitem.title: USA: IMF/World Bank say global economy on the upswing.
newsitem.headline: IMF/World Bank say global economy on the upswing.

text.p: The head of the International Monetary Fund on Tuesday said the global economy had taken a less perilous course of late but cautioned that economic caretakers must not let down their guard.

IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus said the world economy was on the upswing and some of the worst crises of recent times, including staggering problems in Russia and Mexico, had been stifled by prompt international action.

"World economic and financial conditions are generally satisfactory and the outlook is favourable," Camdessus said. "Among the more positive developments, I would cite the reduction in world inflation."
Camdessus spoke at the opening plenary session of the IMF and World Bank annual meeting.
He painted a picture of a highly integrated world economy that provides blessings as well as dangers with the threat of problems in one country easily infecting its global neighbours.

"We know that forces of globilization can magnify the adverse effects of policy weaknesss, pose new risks for all our countries, and raised difficult policy dilemmas even when policies are sound," he said.
"All these considerations impel us to greater vigilence and renewed partnership in facing this new world," he added.
The opening session of the plenary also heard from U.S. Vice President Al Gore, who pledged his country's continued commitment to the international institutions.

Gore told the meeting the Clinton administration would do all it could to meet the country's pledge to the International Development Association, the World Bank's concessional lending arm. The United States is behind in payments to the IDA because Congress, citing budget considerations, has kept a tight rein on spending for international institutions.

Gore, who has criticised the World Bank and other multilateral development banks in the past for not doing enough to protect the environment, also welcomed the progress that has been made on that front recently.
"I welcome the great distance that has been travelled," he said. But, he added, "The really hard work now remains."

As he has in the past, Camdessus lectured countries to live more within their means, be more aggressive in dealing with budget deficits that continue to be a drag on sustained economic vitality and make their economies more efficient.

"In every country we can point to ways in which comprehensive structural reform -- not just tinkering at the margin with this measure or that -- would improve the effectiveness of macroeconomic policies," he said.
But the head of the IMF also showed that the tough lending institution, sometimes regarded as a unfeeling global monetary policeman, had a human side.

"Fiscal adjustment must not only reduce budget deficits, but also improve the quality of expenditure by reducing unproductive outlays to make room for spending on such critical areas as health and education," he said.

But Camdessus and World Bank President James Wolfensohn also made clear that the unfinished agenda, including a global banking system that threatened to unravel in many countries, was being addressed.
Calling it the Achilles heel of the global economy, Camdessus said "a banking crisis is an accident waiting to happen."

Wolfensohn said about one in five developing nations faces a banking crisis. "That is why the Bank group -- working with the IMF -- is strengthening our capacity to help our clients strengthen their financial sectors," he told delegates.
Both Camdessus and Wolfensohn lashed out at corruption in many countries, saying the entrenched practice is weakening the entire system.
"We need to deal with the cancer of corruption," Wolfensohn said, adding, "the Bank group will not tolerate corruption in the programmes that we support."
Camdessus said the progress that has taken place in recent years in many parts of the world was not without cost.
He said that it was critical that the IMF's coffers be refilled as the international lending institution was fast approaching funding levels that were disturbingly low.
He has called for a doubling of IMF resources to about $440 billion but many industrial countries trying to slim down their budget deficits will probably think that is too generous.
